title: Abou v. Alessandra — swimming-pool conformity, partial judicial excerpt
citation: Cour de cassation, 3e civ., January 17, 1984, no. 82-15.982; RTD civ. 1984.711
lead: An owner asks for the four pool steps promised by contract; the reviewing court requires an inquiry into possible performance rather than proof that three steps impaired access.

actors.name: M. Abou
actors.role: Pool owner seeking conformity with the contractual specification.

actors.name: M. Alessandra
actors.role: Party against whom Abou sought corrective performance.

proceedings: The Aix-en-Provence Court of Appeal rejected the conformity request on May 13, 1982.
The reproduced cassation excerpt quashes within the limits of the first ground; the complete order remains unavailable.
limits: Only a partial actual judicial excerpt and the assigned account are available. Other grounds, complete remand terms, costs, judicial author, votes and any omitted writings remain unknown. Adjacent construction cases and later proportionality reforms are distinct.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The agreement specifies four steps for access to the pool
sections.cue: What departure did the owner challenge?
paragraphs: A contractual estimate dated December 26, 1977 specified an access stairway to a swimming pool with four steps, each 0.20 metres high. The owner, M. Abou, sought useful works and conformity of the pool and its accessories from M. Alessandra. The stairway actually had three steps instead of the agreed four.

The available account does not give the contract price, the rest of the construction chronology, other defects or all claims. The particular disagreement preserved here concerns enforcement of that stairway specification.

sources.pinpoint: Agreement and correction; Paris 8 materials, p.193, Document 2

sections.title: Aix-en-Provence requires proof that access became more difficult
sections.cue: Why did Abou challenge that reasoning?
paragraphs: On May 13, 1982, the Aix-en-Provence Court of Appeal rejected the owner’s request for conformity. It reasoned that he had not proved that the change made access to the pool more difficult.

Abou’s first ground of appeal attacked that refusal as a failure to enforce the signed contractual specification. His objection concerned the promised configuration itself, even without proof of worse access. The ground’s argument was then considered by the Court of Cassation’s Third Civil Chamber.

sources.pinpoint: Agreement and lower-court decision; Paris 8, p.193, Document 2

sections.title: The reviewing court asks whether conformity was impossible
sections.cue: Which legal inquiry had the lower court omitted?
paragraphs: The Court of Cassation invoked former Civil Code article 1184. It stated that a party whose undertaking had not been performed could compel performance when performance remained possible.

The lower court had rejected correction because Abou had not shown impaired access, without investigating whether bringing the stairway into conformity was impossible. That missing inquiry deprived its decision of a legal basis. The reproduced reasoning therefore made possible performance the relevant question; it did not make reduced usability a prerequisite to enforcing the agreed number of steps.

sections.title: The first ground succeeds, while the rest of the order is unavailable
sections.cue: What result can actually be stated from the excerpt?
paragraphs: The January 17, 1984 excerpt quashes and annuls the Aix-en-Provence decision within the limits of the first ground. It does not reproduce a complete remand designation, costs ruling or decision on the omitted grounds. It supplies no completed construction order or monetary award by the Court of Cassation.

The assigned English discussion uses the case to illustrate strong enforcement of promised performance. The actual French excerpt gives the narrower procedural explanation:the lower court had to investigate impossibility. Nearby examples about a house’s height or alignment concern other decisions, and the later debate about a proportionality exception does not form part of this 1984 ruling.
